LESSON: RHYTHM

Grade: SNE  /  physical-impairment / Grade 9
Subject: CREATIVE ARTS AND SPORTS
Strand: Creating and Performing
Topic 2.2: Rhythm
Suggested lessons in curriculum: 10

SECTION 1: INTRODUCTION

This lesson covers Rhythm, part of Creating and Performing in SNE  /  physical-impairment / Grade 9 CREATIVE ARTS AND SPORTS.

Key inquiry question: when demonstrating using the model 1. How are various note combinations used to form rhythms in simple time?

You will study the official KICD learning outcomes, classroom activities, values, and competencies for this topic. Use Kenyan examples from your county, school, and community throughout.

SECTION 2: LEARNING OUTCOMES

By the end of this topic, you should be able to:

A. describe the effect of note extension on rhythmic patterns,

   Learning focus: This outcome is part of Rhythm in the Kenya CBC curriculum.
   In class: Your teacher will guide you to discuss, practise, and demonstrate this skill using examples from Kenya.
   At home: Explain this point to a parent using an example from your school, home, or community.

B. compose a four--bar rhythmic patterns in 4 4 time,

   Learning focus: This outcome is part of Rhythm in the Kenya CBC curriculum.
   In class: Your teacher will guide you to discuss, practise, and demonstrate this skill using examples from Kenya.
   At home: Explain this point to a parent using an example from your school, home, or community.

C. notate four-bar rhythms in 4 4 time,

   Learning focus: This outcome is part of Rhythm in the Kenya CBC curriculum.
   In class: Your teacher will guide you to discuss, practise, and demonstrate this skill using examples from Kenya.
   At home: Explain this point to a parent using an example from your school, home, or community.

D. create rhythmic patterns in 4 4 time for synchronised movements in basketball routines,

   Learning focus: This outcome is part of Rhythm in the Kenya CBC curriculum.
   In class: Your teacher will guide you to discuss, practise, and demonstrate this skill using examples from Kenya.
   At home: Explain this point to a parent using an example from your school, home, or community.

E. appreciate rhythmic patterns as a means of creating interest in Creative Arts and Sports.

   Learning focus: This outcome is part of Rhythm in the Kenya CBC curriculum.
   In class: Your teacher will guide you to discuss, practise, and demonstrate this skill using examples from Kenya.
   At home: Explain this point to a parent using an example from your school, home, or community.

SECTION 3: KEY CONCEPTS AND EXPLANATION

A. describe the effect of note extension on rhythmic patterns,

   Rhythm helps learners achieve this outcome through discussion, practice, and activities at school. Think about how this applies in daily life in Kenya — at home, on the farm, in town, or at school.

B. compose a four--bar rhythmic patterns in 4 4 time,

   Rhythm helps learners achieve this outcome through discussion, practice, and activities at school. Think about how this applies in daily life in Kenya — at home, on the farm, in town, or at school.

C. notate four-bar rhythms in 4 4 time,

   Rhythm helps learners achieve this outcome through discussion, practice, and activities at school. Think about how this applies in daily life in Kenya — at home, on the farm, in town, or at school.

D. create rhythmic patterns in 4 4 time for synchronised movements in basketball routines,

   Rhythm helps learners achieve this outcome through discussion, practice, and activities at school. Think about how this applies in daily life in Kenya — at home, on the farm, in town, or at school.

E. appreciate rhythmic patterns as a means of creating interest in Creative Arts and Sports.

   Rhythm helps learners achieve this outcome through discussion, practice, and activities at school. Think about how this applies in daily life in Kenya — at home, on the farm, in town, or at school.

F. Suggested learning experiences (from KICD)

1. Listen to, sing or play tunes involving dotted notes to outline effects of note extension in rhythmic patterns. Learners with speech difficulties could use residual speech, hum, mime or use alternative modes of communication.

2. Beat time to familiar tunes in 4 4 time considering the crochet as principle beat, accented and weak beats. Learners with manipulation difficulties could use alternative functional parts of the body or use assistive technology

SECTION 4: LEARNING ACTIVITIES

A. At school

1. Listen to, sing or play tunes involving dotted notes to outline effects of note extension in rhythmic patterns. Learners with speech difficulties could use residual speech, hum, mime or use alternative modes of communication.
2. Beat time to familiar tunes in 4 4 time considering the crochet as principle beat, accented and weak beats. Learners with manipulation difficulties could use alternative functional parts of the body or use assistive technology

B. At home with your parent or guardian

1. Read this lesson on Rhythm together.
2. Discuss the key inquiry question and give examples from your area.
3. Write five sentences summarising what you learned.
4. Prepare for the revision quiz at the end of this topic.

SECTION 5: CORE COMPETENCIES, VALUES, AND PCIs

Core Competencies to be developed:
• Communication and Collaboration: The learner, through effective communication, articulates and discusses the effect of

note extension in rhythmic patterns, with peers.

• Learning to Learn: The learner actively seeks to understand and apply notation conventions to represent rhythm in music.

• Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: The learner creatively solves problems related to achieving the desired solutions on

rhythmic structure in creating rhythmic patterns,

• Creativity and Imagination: The learner embraces creativity by exploring innovative factors such as unconventional

instruments, unique combinations of beats, or experimental rhythmic elements as they create rhythmic patterns.

Values:

• Peace: the learner while engaging in the creative process of composing a rhythm fosters a peaceful state of mind, allowing

free and peaceful expression through music.

• Unity: the learner in collaborating with others on rhythm composition projects creates a harmonious atmosphere.

• Responsibility: the learner takes responsibility for their part in the ensemble while playing in unison or in two-part music,

ensuring a coordinated and responsible musical performance.

• Social Justice: the learner in creating, improvising and notating rhythms with diverse influences - notation and interaction

with games- contributes to social justice by acknowledging and celebrating cultural diversity in music.
